unit.title: Use graphical techniques and perform simple statistical computations (Basic)

summary: This unit teaches you to collect workshop data, such as job times, readings and fault logs, and turn it into tables, graphs and simple statistics. You will learn to make tally charts and frequency tables, work out the mean, median, mode and range, work with percentages, and draw and read bar charts, pie charts, histograms, line graphs and scatter graphs. You will also learn to check your work and write a short report on what the results show.

blocks.p: Electricians collect numbers all the time: how long jobs take, test readings, the faults found each month, energy used, temperatures of motors and panels. On their own, long lists of numbers are hard to understand. Arranged in a table, shown on a graph and summed up with a few simple statistics, they show what is normal, what is changing and where the problems are. This unit is for Level 2 trainees and is shared by several engineering trades, so the methods work for any kind of workshop data.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like in the workshop
rows: Decide what to measure, design a record sheet, and write each reading or event down straight away, in the same way each time.
Sort data with tallies and frequency tables
Count how often each value or type occurs, in single values or in groups, and check the total.
Find the mean, median, mode and range, and say what each tells you.
Work out a percentage of a total, a percentage change, and change between fractions, decimals and percentages.
Pick a bar chart, pie chart, histogram, line graph or scatter graph to suit the data and the question.
Use equal scales, labelled axes with units, a title and accurate plotting.
Read values, see trends and links, and spot misleading graphs.
Check data and calculations for mistakes, deal with unusual values, and write clear statements about what the results show.

ul: A calculator, graph paper, a sharp pencil, an eraser and a ruler.
A pair of compasses and a protractor for pie charts.
Record sheets, and where the Centre allows, a spreadsheet on a computer.
Patience: most mistakes in statistics are copying and counting slips, not hard sums.

blocks.p: Read the sections in order, and work every example yourself with a calculator before you read the answer. Then try the practice test and read every explanation. Your instructor will give you real data from the Centre's workshop to practise on.

Before collecting anything, decide **what you need to find out** and **what to measure or count**. 'Which faults happen most in the workshop?' needs a count of faults by type. 'How long does it take to wire a socket outlet?' needs timed jobs. 'Do older motors break down more?' needs pairs of values: each motor's age and its number of faults.

head: Kind
What it is
Examples
Shown best by
rows: Names or types that are counted
Fault types, cable colours, which machine, which trade
Values measured on a scale, with units

ul: Has a title, the date, the place and the name of the person recording.
Has clear columns, each with a heading and a **unit**: 'Time (min)', 'Resistance (Ω)'.
Uses agreed categories, so that two people record the same fault the same way ('breaker trip', not 'breaker' one day and 'tripping' the next).
Has space for notes, such as 'meter battery changed' or 'job interrupted'.
Write each reading down **as soon as it is taken**, so it is not forgotten or mixed up.
Take readings **the same way each time**: the same instrument, the same point, the same method. Then they can be compared fairly.
Record the value as it is shown. Do not round it to a 'nicer' number, and never make up a reading you missed: leave a gap and note why.
Take enough readings. One or two timed jobs tell you little; ten or more give a much better picture.

head: Mistake
Example
How to catch it
rows: The value is ten times the others
Check against the instrument while it still shows the value
A reading in kΩ written as Ω
Write the unit with every reading
A value copied wrongly from the rough sheet
Check copied tables against the original
A fault entered on two days
Check the total against the number of entries

blocks.p: An **outlier** is a value much higher or lower than all the others. It may be a **mistake** (a slip in reading or writing), or it may be **real** (a faulty part, a job that hit a problem). Never just delete it. First check whether it is a mistake and correct it if you can, for example by measuring again. If it is real, find out why it happened, keep it, and mention it in your report.

A **tally** counts things as you go down a list. Draw one upright stroke for each item. The **fifth** stroke is drawn **across** the first four, making a 'gate' that stands for 5. Then the tally can be counted quickly in fives.
**Example.** A month's fault log is tallied by type. Lamp faults: two gates and three strokes = 5 + 5 + 3 = **13**.

The **frequency** is how many times something occurs. A frequency table lists each category or value with its frequency. Always add up the frequencies and **check the total** against the number of entries on the record sheet.
When measurements are spread over many values, such as 25 job times between 11 and 34 minutes, put them into **groups** (classes) of equal width.

ul: Use about 5 to 8 groups: too few hide the pattern, too many leave most groups nearly empty.
Make the groups the **same width**, with **no gaps and no overlaps**. For whole minutes: 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34. A time of 15 goes in 15–19.
For values with decimals, write the groups so that every value has one place: 10 ≤ t < 15 means from 10 up to, but not including, 15.
Groups like 10–15 and 15–20 overlap: a time of 15 would fit both. Do not use them.

blocks.note: Add a **percentage** column to a frequency table: each frequency ÷ total × 100. The percentages should add up to 100% (or very close, after rounding). It makes tables of different sizes easy to compare.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: An **average** gives one value that represents a whole set. There are three kinds, and each tells you something different. The **range** tells you how spread out the values are.

head: Measure
How to find it
What it tells you
rows: Add all the values and divide by how many there are
The usual 'average'. Uses every value, so one unusual value can pull it a long way.
Put the values in order of size and take the middle one
The middle value: half are below it and half above. Hardly affected by one unusual value.
The value (or category) that occurs most often
The most common value. The only average that works for categories, such as fault types.
The largest value minus the smallest
How spread out the values are. A big range means results vary a lot.

blocks.h: Worked example: an odd number of values

blocks.p: Seven trainees took these times, in minutes, to wire a two-way lighting circuit: **34, 29, 31, 40, 29, 33, 35**.

ul: **Median:** in order: 29, 29, 31, 33, 34, 35, 40. With 7 values, the middle is the 4th: **33 min**.
**Mode:** 29 occurs twice, more than any other: **29 min**.

blocks.h: Worked example: an even number of values

ul: **Median:** in order: 21.8, 21.9, 22.0, 22.1, 22.4, 22.6. With 6 values there are two middle values (the 3rd and 4th): 22.0 and 22.1. The median is half-way between them: (22.0 + 22.1) ÷ 2 = **22.05 Ω**.
**Mode:** every value occurs once, so there is **no mode**. A set can also have two modes.

blocks.note: The middle position of an ordered list is (n + 1) ÷ 2, where n is the number of values. For 7 values it is the 4th; for 10 values it is 5.5, meaning half-way between the 5th and 6th.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.h: The mean from a frequency table

blocks.p: When a table shows how many times each value occurred, multiply each value by its frequency, add the results, and divide by the total frequency.
Mean = 51 ÷ 30 = **1.7 call-outs per day**. Dividing by 5 (the number of rows) instead of 30 (the number of days) is a common mistake.

blocks.h: The effect of an unusual value

blocks.p: Repair times of 3, 4, 4, 5 and 34 hours: the mean is 50 ÷ 5 = 10 hours, which is more than four of the five repairs took. The median is 4 hours, which is much more typical. The range (31 hours) is also made large by the one value. When a set has an outlier, give the median as well as the mean, and explain the unusual value.

blocks.note: Quick checks: the mean and median must lie **between** the smallest and largest values; the range can never be negative; and the mode must be one of the values in the set.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **percentage** is a number out of 100. Percentages let you compare parts of different-sized wholes: 6 faults out of 40 and 9 out of 75 are easier to compare as 15% and 12%.

head: To do this
Method
Example
rows: Find what percentage one number is of another
Find a percentage of an amount
Change a decimal to a percentage
Change a percentage to a decimal
Change a fraction to a percentage

blocks.p: **Percentage change = change ÷ starting value × 100.** Always divide by the **starting** (old) value.

ul: **Rise:** outlet faults went from 20 in May to 26 in June. Change = 6. 6 ÷ 20 × 100 = **30% rise**.
**Fall:** call-outs went from 60 to 45. Change = 15. 15 ÷ 60 × 100 = **25% fall**. (Dividing by 45, the new value, would give 33%, which is wrong.)
**Over-run:** a job planned at 15 hours took 18. 3 ÷ 15 × 100 = **20% over** the plan.
'**Times as many**' means divide: 24 faults on line A and 6 on line B means A had 24 ÷ 6 = 4 times as many as B.
'**More than**' means take away: A had 24 − 6 = 18 more faults than B.
A **ratio** compares parts: 24 : 6 simplifies to 4 : 1.

blocks.note: Sense-check every percentage: a part of a whole cannot be more than 100%; 1/4 is 25%, 1/2 is 50%, 3/4 is 75%. If 9 out of 150 lamps failed, the answer must be small (6%), not 60%.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Drawing graphs: axes, scales and labels

head: Part
What it must have
rows: Says what the graph shows, where and when: 'Motor 3 casing temperature after start-up, 4 March'.
Usually the thing that is set or that passes steadily, such as time, or the categories in a bar chart.
Usually what is measured or counted, such as temperature or number of faults.
The quantity and its **unit** on each axis: 'Time (min)', 'Temperature (°C)', 'Number of faults'.
Numbers that go up in **equal steps**, marked clearly.
Needed when colours or symbols stand for different things.

flow: Find the smallest and largest values to be plotted
Count the large squares available on each axis
Divide the spread of values by the number of squares
Round up to an easy step: 1, 2, 5 or 10 (or 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 20, 50, 100...)
Check the graph will fill at least half of the paper in each direction

blocks.p: **Example.** Values from 0 to 37 must fit on 8 large squares. 37 ÷ 8 = 4.6, so use **5 per large square**, from 0 to 40. A step of 4.6 or 7 per square would make values very hard to plot and read.

ul: **Equal steps:** if the steps are uneven, the shape of the graph is wrong and misleads the reader.
**Fill the paper:** a large graph can be plotted and read more accurately than a tiny one in a corner.

**Start bar charts at zero.** For a line graph whose values are all far from zero, such as temperatures between 60 and 80 °C, the axis may start near the lowest value, but show a small zig-zag on the axis to mark the break.
Use a sharp pencil. Mark each point with a small, neat cross (×) or dot exactly at its value.
Read across from the y-value and up from the x-value; check each point against the table afterwards.
Draw lines with a ruler, unless a smooth curve is clearly the right shape.

head: Trick
Why it misleads
rows: Bar chart axis that does not start at zero
A small difference looks huge: 46 and 48 look like 1 and 3 if the axis starts at 45.
Changes the shape of a line, so trends look steeper or flatter than they are.
The reader cannot tell what is measured or how big it is.
Front sectors look bigger than back ones of the same size.
The eye compares areas, not just heights.

sections.title: Bar charts, pie charts and histograms

blocks.p: A **bar chart** compares separate categories. Each category has a bar whose **height** shows its amount. All the bars are the **same width**, with **equal gaps** between them, so that only the height carries the information.

flow: Start from the frequency table and check its total
Draw the axes: categories along the bottom, amounts up the side
Choose an equal scale from zero that fits the largest amount and fills the paper
Label both axes, with units where needed
Draw equal-width bars with equal gaps, to the right heights
Add a title, and a key if colours stand for something
Check each bar against the table

ul: **Bars in order**: drawing the bars from the most to the fewest (a **Pareto chart**) shows at once which categories matter most, so that effort goes where it will cut the most faults.
**Grouped bars**: two bars side by side for each category (for example this month and last month, in two colours with a key) compare two sets.
**Reading values**: if the scale goes up in steps of 2 and a bar ends half-way between 10 and 12, it shows 11.

blocks.p: A **pie chart** shows how **one whole** is shared into parts. Each part is a **sector** whose angle is in proportion to its share. A full circle is **360°**.
**Angle of a sector = frequency ÷ total × 360°.** Or work out the angle for one item first: 360 ÷ total, then multiply.

flow: Work out every angle and check they add up to 360°
Draw a circle with compasses and mark its centre
Draw one radius (centre to edge) as a starting line
Put the protractor's centre on the circle's centre and its zero line on the radius; mark the first angle and draw the next radius
Measure each following angle from the last line drawn
Label each sector (type and number or percentage), or colour it and add a key; add a title

ul: A percentage turns into an angle by multiplying by 3.6 (because 360 ÷ 100 = 3.6): 25% = 90°.
Some angle fractions to know: 180° is a half, 90° a quarter, 120° a third, 72° a fifth, 45° an eighth.
If rounding makes the angles add to 359° or 361°, adjust the largest sector by one degree.
Pie charts work best with a few categories (about 6 or fewer). They are poor for reading exact values or comparing two months: use a bar chart for that.

blocks.p: A **histogram** shows **grouped measurements**, such as job times grouped 10–14, 15–19, 20–24 minutes. It looks like a bar chart, but the **bars touch**, because the groups follow on from each other with no gaps on the number scale. The horizontal axis is a number scale (the measurement), and the height of each bar is the frequency of that group (when the groups are of equal width).

head: Feature
Bar chart
Histogram
rows: Category names; order can be changed
A number scale; order is fixed

blocks.p: The shape of a histogram tells a story: a tall middle with low sides means most jobs take about the same time; a long tail to the right means a few jobs take much longer, and their causes are worth finding.

A **line graph** shows how one measured value **changes over time** (or as another value is steadily changed). Time goes along the horizontal axis. Each reading is plotted as a point and the points are joined, so the line shows the **trend**.

flow: Record readings in a table of time and value, at regular times
Put time on the horizontal axis and the measured value on the vertical axis
Choose equal scales that fit the data and fill the paper; label both axes with units
Plot each point exactly; join the points with straight lines or a smooth curve
Add a title

ul: **Reading between points (interpolation):** to find the value at a time between two readings, go up from that time to the line, then across to the vertical axis. If the line is straight between two points, the value half-way in time is half-way between the two values.

**Trend:** a line rising, falling, levelling off or going up and down. A motor that warms up quickly and then levels off has reached its steady running temperature; one that keeps climbing may be overloaded.
**Rate of change:** the change in value ÷ the change in time. A rise from 30 °C to 46 °C in 8 minutes is 16 ÷ 8 = 2 °C per minute. A steeper line means a faster change.
**Beyond the data (extrapolation):** extending the line past the last reading is only a guess, because the trend may change. Say so if you do it.

blocks.p: A **scatter graph** shows whether two measurements are **linked**. Each item gives a pair of values, such as a cable's length and its voltage drop, or a motor's age and its number of faults. Each pair is plotted as one point. The points are **not joined**.

head: Pattern of points
Name
Meaning
rows: As one value increases, the other tends to increase.
As one value increases, the other tends to decrease.
No clear link between the two.

ul: The closer the points lie to a straight line, the **stronger** the link; a loose cloud is a weak link.

A **line of best fit** is a straight line drawn through the middle of the points, following their direction, with about as many points above it as below. It does not have to pass through any particular point, or through zero.
Use the line of best fit to **estimate** a value: go up from one value to the line, then across.
A point far from the others is an **outlier**: check it, find out why, and leave it out when drawing the line if it was caused by something unusual.
**A link does not prove a cause.** Two things can rise together because a third thing affects both. Use the graph as evidence to look into, not as proof.

head: Check
How
rows: Compare your table with the original record sheet; check that the totals match the number of entries.
Do each one again, if possible another way: add a column from the bottom up; work a percentage back the other way.
Mean and median between the smallest and largest values; percentages of a whole add to 100%; pie angles add to 360°.
Title, both axes labelled with units, equal scales, key if needed; check a few points or bars against the table.
Clear handwriting and labels; no crossings-out that hide values.
Ask another member of the group to check your work; check theirs in return.

blocks.p: A short report turns graphs and numbers into a few clear statements that someone can act on. Write facts the data supports, with the numbers, then any suggestions.

ul: **The biggest or most common:** 'Lamp faults were the most common: 14 of the 40 faults (35%).'
**Comparisons:** 'Line A had 4 times as many faults as line B.'
**Trends:** 'Outlet faults rose for the third month in a row, from 20 to 26 (a 30% rise).'
**Spread and unusual values:** 'Most jobs took 20 to 24 minutes; one took 34 minutes because a box had to be refixed.'
**Suggestions:** 'Fit longer-life lamps in the corridor, where most lamp faults occur.'

blocks.note: Do not claim more than the data shows. 'Faults rose in hot months' is a fact from the data; 'the heat causes faults' is a guess that needs more evidence. Report trends early, so that causes can be found and fixed.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A spreadsheet can store the data, work out statistics and draw charts. Functions with names such as AVERAGE (the mean), MEDIAN, MODE, MIN, MAX and COUNT are found in most spreadsheets; the range is MAX minus MIN. A spreadsheet only works with what it is given, so check that the data was typed in correctly, that each formula covers the right cells, and that every chart has a title, labels and sensible scales.

**Workshop faults, March.** 40 faults were logged (32 in February, a 25% rise). Lamps were the most common type (14, 35%), followed by outlets (10, 25%). Breaker trips rose from 4 to 8, all on the bench-grinder circuit. The mean repair time was 1.6 hours; the median was 1.0 hour, because two motor repairs took over 6 hours. Suggestions: check the bench-grinder circuit and the grinders on it; keep a stock of the lamp type that fails most.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can decide what data to collect, design a record sheet and record readings straight away, in the same way each time.
I can spot and deal with recording mistakes and outliers without just deleting them.
I can tally data and make a frequency table, and check its total.
I can group measurements into equal groups with no gaps or overlaps.
I can work out the mean, median, mode and range, for odd and even numbers of values.
I can work out a mean from a frequency table.
I can explain how an outlier affects the mean, the median and the range.
I can work out a percentage of a whole, a percentage of an amount and a percentage change.
I can change between fractions, decimals and percentages.
I can choose the right graph for a set of data.
I can choose a scale, label axes with units, add a title and plot accurately.
I can draw and read a bar chart, with bars in order when that helps.
I can work out pie chart angles, check they total 360°, and draw the chart with compasses and a protractor.
I can draw a histogram and explain how it differs from a bar chart.
I can draw a line graph, read values between points and describe the trend.
I can draw a scatter graph, describe the correlation and draw a line of best fit.
I can spot a misleading graph.
I can check my work and write clear statements about what the results show.

head: Formula
Use
rows: Mean = total of values ÷ number of values

terms: A chart of separate categories, with bars of equal width and gaps between them.
A link between two measurements: positive, negative or none.
Facts collected for a purpose, such as counts and readings.
How many times a value or category occurs.
A table listing each value or category with its frequency.
A chart of grouped measurements, with touching bars on a number scale.
Reading a value between two plotted points.
Points plotted against time (or a steadily changing value) and joined to show a trend.
A straight line through the middle of the points on a scatter graph, showing the trend.
The total of the values divided by how many there are.
The middle value when the values are in order of size.
The value or category that occurs most often.
A value much higher or lower than the others.
A bar chart with the bars in order from largest to smallest.
A circle divided into sectors whose angles show the shares of a whole.
The largest value minus the smallest: a measure of spread.
A graph of pairs of values, plotted as unjoined points, to show whether they are linked.
A slice of a pie chart.
Counting marks drawn in gates of five.
The general direction in which values change.
The horizontal axis / the vertical axis of a graph.

c1.title: Timing outlet boxes on a Hellshire housing scheme
c1.text: On a new housing scheme at Hellshire, St Catherine, site supervisor Mr Lloyd Bennett wants to know how long it takes to fit and terminate one 110 V outlet, so that he can price the next phase. Trainee Ashani times ten outlets fitted by the team. Her times, in minutes, are: 18, 22, 19, 25, 21, 19, 24, 19, 20, 23.

c2.title: A month's faults at a Discovery Bay hotel
c2.text: The maintenance team at a hotel in Discovery Bay, St Ann, logged 48 electrical faults in September: lamps 18, air-conditioning units 12, outlets 8, breaker trips 6 and other faults 4. In August they logged 32 faults. Trainee Kerone is preparing charts and a short report for the chief engineer, Mrs Dahlia Morgan.

c3.title: A conveyor motor at a Spanish Town packaging plant
c3.text: At a packaging plant in Spanish Town, St Catherine, trainee Odessa records the casing temperature of a conveyor motor with an infrared thermometer, from a safe position, every 10 minutes after start-up. Her readings are: 0 min 31 °C, 10 min 42 °C, 20 min 50 °C, 30 min 55 °C, 40 min 58 °C, 50 min 59 °C and 60 min 59 °C. She will plot them as a line graph.

c4.title: Hot days and power use at a Lucea supermarket
c4.text: The manager of a supermarket in Lucea, Hanover, asks the maintenance trainee, Garfield, whether hotter days really use more electricity. For 20 days Garfield records the highest outdoor temperature and the energy used that day, read from the supermarket's meter in kWh. He plots the pairs as a scatter graph. The points rise from left to right in a fairly narrow band, except for one day at 33 °C when the energy used was far lower than on other hot days.

c5.title: New heater elements at a Falmouth workshop
c5.text: A workshop in Falmouth, Trelawny, has bought ten replacement water heater elements marked 16 Ω ±5%. Trainee Romaine measures each one with an ohmmeter, with no supply connected, and records these values in ohms: 15.9, 16.1, 16.3, 15.8, 16.0, 161, 16.2, 15.7, 17.1, 16.0.

questions.q: What is the mean of Ashani's ten times?
o: 19 min
20.5 min
21 min
210 min
questions.why: Add the times: 18 + 22 + 19 + 25 + 21 + 19 + 24 + 19 + 20 + 23 = 210. Divide by the number of times: 210 ÷ 10 = 21 minutes. 210 is the total, 20.5 is the median and 19 is the mode.

questions.q: What is the median of Ashani's times?
o: 20 min
20.5 min
21 min
21.5 min
questions.why: In order: 18, 19, 19, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 24, 25. With ten values there are two middle ones, the 5th (20) and the 6th (21). The median is half-way between them: 20.5 minutes.

questions.q: Ashani groups the times as 18–19, 20–21, 22–23 and 24–25 minutes. What is the frequency of the 18–19 group?
questions.why: The times 18, 19, 19 and 19 fall in the 18–19 group, so its frequency is 4. The other groups have 2 each, and 4 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 10 checks against the ten times recorded.

questions.q: Which statement about the times is supported by the data?
o: Most of the outlets took exactly 21 minutes each
Half the outlets took 20.5 minutes or less
No outlet took longer than 21 minutes
The times were spread from 18 to 21 minutes
questions.why: The median, 20.5 minutes, splits the times in half: five are below it and five above. The most common time (the mode) was 19 minutes, not 21, and the times ran from 18 to 25 minutes, a range of 7.

questions.q: What angle should the air-conditioning sector have on Kerone's pie chart?
questions.why: Angle = frequency ÷ total × 360° = 12 ÷ 48 × 360 = 90°. Air-conditioning faults are a quarter of all the faults, and a quarter of a circle is 90°.

questions.q: What percentage of September's faults were lamp faults?
questions.why: Percentage = part ÷ whole × 100 = 18 ÷ 48 × 100 = 37.5%. 18% confuses the number of faults with the percentage, and 62.5% is the share of all the other faults.

questions.q: By what percentage did the number of faults change from August to September?
o: A 33% rise
A 16% rise
A 150% rise
A 50% rise
questions.why: Change = 48 − 32 = 16. Divide by the starting value, August's 32: 16 ÷ 32 × 100 = 50% rise. Dividing by 48, the new value, gives the wrong answer of 33%.

questions.q: Mrs Morgan wants to see at a glance which fault types to tackle first. Which chart suits this best?
o: A line graph joining the five fault types
A bar chart with bars in order, largest first
A scatter graph of faults against fault type
A histogram with the fault-type bars touching
questions.why: A bar chart compares separate categories, and putting the bars in order (a Pareto chart) shows at once which types cause most faults. A line graph is for change over time, a scatter graph for pairs of measurements and a histogram for grouped measurements.

questions.q: From Odessa's line graph, about what was the motor's temperature 25 minutes after start-up?
o: About 50 °C
About 55 °C
About 53 °C
About 58 °C
questions.why: 25 minutes is half-way between the readings at 20 minutes (50 °C) and 30 minutes (55 °C). Reading from the line, the value is about half-way between them: about 52 to 53 °C.

questions.q: Which statement describes the trend in Odessa's readings?
o: It rose steadily by about the same amount every 10 minutes
It rose to a peak and then fell back towards 31 °C
It kept climbing, so the motor is overheating
It rose quickly at first, then levelled off at about 59 °C
questions.why: The rises get smaller: 11, 8, 5, 3, 1 and then 0 °C per 10 minutes. The line climbs steeply and then flattens at about 59 °C, which is the motor's steady running temperature. A line that kept climbing would be a warning.

questions.q: At what average rate did the motor's temperature rise during the first 10 minutes?
o: 11 °C per minute
4.2 °C per minute
1.1 °C per minute
0.9 °C per minute
questions.why: Rate of change = change in temperature ÷ change in time = (42 − 31) ÷ 10 = 11 ÷ 10 = 1.1 °C per minute. Later the rise slows, and the line on the graph becomes less steep.

questions.q: What does the pattern of Garfield's points show?
o: No link between temperature and energy used
Hotter days tend to use less electricity
Each 1 °C rise doubles the energy used
Hotter days tend to use more electricity
questions.why: Points rising from left to right in a narrow band show a strong positive correlation: as the temperature goes up, the energy used tends to go up, probably because air-conditioning and refrigeration work harder. The graph shows a link, not an exact rule such as doubling.

questions.q: What should Garfield do about the day at 33 °C with very low energy use?
o: Find out why: perhaps the store closed or power failed
Delete it, because it spoils the pattern of the graph
Change it to match the other hot days on the graph
Draw the line of best fit so that it passes through it
questions.why: An outlier must be checked, not deleted or changed. A power cut, a short trading day or a misread meter could explain it. If the cause was something unusual, note it and leave it out when drawing the line of best fit.

questions.q: How should Garfield draw the line of best fit?
o: A straight line from the first point to the last point
A line from zero through the highest point plotted
Lines joining every point in order, dot to dot
A straight line through the middle of the points
questions.why: A line of best fit follows the direction of the points through their middle, with about as many points above it as below. It need not pass through any particular point, nor through zero. Joining the dots is for a line graph, not a scatter graph.

questions.q: Before working out any statistics, what should Romaine do about the value 161?
o: Measure that element again and correct the record
Leave it, since every reading must be kept as written
Delete it and work with the nine other values
Replace it with the mean of the other nine values
questions.why: 161 is ten times the other readings, so it is probably a missed decimal point, but that must be checked, not assumed. Measuring the element again gives its true value. Leaving 161 in would wreck the mean and range; deleting it or inventing a value loses a real element.

questions.q: The sixth element measures 16.1 Ω when checked again. How many elements are outside the 16 Ω ±5% tolerance?
questions.why: 5% of 16 Ω is 0.8 Ω, so the limits are 15.2 Ω to 16.8 Ω. Only 17.1 Ω is outside. Counting the uncorrected 161 as a failure as well would wrongly give 2.

questions.q: Using 16.1 Ω for the sixth element, what is the mean resistance, to one decimal place?
questions.why: The corrected values add up to 161.2 Ω. 161.2 ÷ 10 = 16.12, which is 16.1 Ω to one decimal place. With the slip left in, the total is 306.1 and the 'mean' becomes 30.6 Ω, which is larger than nine of the ten readings: a sign that something is wrong.

questions.q: What percentage of the elements failed the tolerance check?
questions.why: One element out of ten failed: 1 ÷ 10 × 100 = 10%. 90% is the share that passed. The failed element should be returned to the supplier.

questions.q: On a fault log, four repairs took 2 h each, five took 3 h each and one took 6 h. What is the mean repair time?
questions.why: Multiply each time by how many repairs took it: 4 × 2 = 8, 5 × 3 = 15, 1 × 6 = 6. Total = 29 hours for 10 repairs, so the mean is 29 ÷ 10 = 2.9 h. Dividing the three times (2 + 3 + 6 = 11) by 3 ignores how often each occurred.

questions.q: A bar chart's vertical axis starts at 40. Team A's bar shows 44 jobs and Team B's 48, and B's bar looks twice as tall. What is wrong with the chart?
o: The bars should touch each other, as in a histogram
Team B's bar has been drawn to the wrong height
The axis starts at 40, so the gap looks far bigger
The chart needs a key to show which team is which
questions.why: B did about 9% more jobs than A (4 more out of 44), not twice as many. Starting a bar chart's axis at 40 cuts off most of each bar, so a small difference looks huge. Bar chart scales should start at zero.
